_about: News page. Add new items at the top of items. verified=true only after someone opened the DOI/URL and checked who, venue, date and every number in gist/plain/tech. Fields: gist (one line), plain (a short story for anyone), tech (for specialists), borrow (what this project takes from it or tests), status (planned, running, done). topic: one of the names in topics (add a new topic only when five or more items need it). field_now: a short summary of where the field is, with library ids (docs/library/library.json).

landscape.method: Counts are estimates from keyword matches in OpenAlex titles and abstracts, journal articles and reviews only, for the 12 months to the update date. A paper can match more than one direction, and the headline removes people counted twice. Distinct authors and institutions are exact up to 400 papers per direction and extrapolated from the newest 400 above that. Each direction lists its exact query so anyone can check it.
landscape.headline: Roughly 6,300 researchers published journal papers on consciousness science in the past year, across these 11 directions.

directions.name: Clinical markers and disorders of consciousness
directions.bet: Measure consciousness at the bedside: complexity indices (PCI), EEG and fMRI to find awareness in patients who cannot respond.

query.search: ("disorders of consciousness" OR "perturbational complexity" OR "vegetative state" OR "minimally conscious state" OR "unresponsive wakefulness" OR "covert consciousness" OR "cognitive motor dissociation")

directions.now: Covert consciousness in patients who look unresponsive is the main push, with bedside EEG and fMRI, and early drug trials aimed at recovery.
directions.us: Our red-teamed benchmark re-scores published consciousness measures, PCI-style complexity included, with splits that cannot leak.

directions.name: Anaesthesia
directions.bet: Switch consciousness off and on with drugs and track what the brain loses and regains.

query.search: (anesthesia OR anaesthesia OR propofol OR sevoflurane OR ketamine) AND (consciousness OR unconsciousness) AND (EEG OR cortical OR brain)

directions.now: Groups map which circuits (thalamus, basal ganglia) switch off under each drug and whether the brain loses integration or only responsiveness.
directions.us: Our time-irreversibility tests on anaesthesia and sleep data found the markers follow arousal, not experience.

directions.name: Sleep and dreaming
directions.bet: Sleep changes experience while the body stays still, so dreaming against dreamless sleep is a natural contrast.

query.search: (dream OR dreaming OR dreams OR "lucid dreaming" OR "sleep mentation" OR "serial awakening") AND sleep AND (EEG OR consciousness OR REM OR NREM OR awakening OR awakenings)

directions.now: Serial-awakening studies with high-density EEG, and real-time reports from dreamers, are mapping what changes in the brain when sleepers report an experience.
directions.us: Our experience benchmark uses the open DREAM database to test whether published measures can tell dreaming from dreamless sleep.

directions.name: Psychedelics
directions.bet: Drugs that change experience a lot without sedation show which brain changes track experience itself.

query.search: (psychedelic OR psychedelics OR psilocybin OR LSD OR DMT OR "5-MeO-DMT") AND (consciousness OR "altered states")

directions.now: Studies link brain changes under psilocybin to how intense the experience is, and test the 'entropic brain' idea against simpler spectral effects.
directions.us: Open psilocybin EEG is one of the contrasts we use to separate experience from arousal.

directions.name: Perception and recurrent processing
directions.bet: Find what changes in the brain when the same stimulus is seen or missed; recurrent processing theory says local feedback in sensory cortex is enough.

query.search: ("recurrent processing" OR "neural correlates of consciousness" OR "conscious perception" OR "visual awareness" OR "conscious access" OR "perceptual awareness" OR "conscious report") AND (consciousness OR conscious OR awareness) AND (brain OR neural OR cortex OR cortical OR EEG OR MEG OR fMRI)

groups.name: Lucia Melloni
groups.inst: Max Planck Institute for Empirical Aesthetics

directions.now: No-report designs and long-timescale dynamics are separating the brain activity that tracks awareness from the activity that tracks reporting it. Some argue that there are several kinds of correlate.
directions.us: Our census of open data with reports counts which awareness datasets can be reused, and with what kind of report.

directions.name: Consciousness in AI
directions.bet: Ask whether machines could be conscious by checking them against the indicators that theories name.

query.search: "artificial consciousness" OR "machine consciousness" OR "AI consciousness" OR "conscious AI" OR "conscious machines" OR "AI sentience" OR "consciousness in large language models" OR "consciousness in artificial"

directions.now: Groups are drawing indicator checklists from brain theories and testing whether language models build workspace-like representations. This is the fastest-growing direction here.

directions.name: Predictive processing and active inference
directions.bet: Experience is the brain's best guess about the causes of its inputs, including the body.

query.search: ("predictive processing" OR "predictive coding" OR "active inference" OR "free energy principle") AND consciousness

directions.now: Active-inference accounts are being turned into concrete predictions, including links to meditation and an adversarial test against IIT.

directions.name: Integrated information theory
directions.bet: Consciousness is how much a system's causal structure is integrated, measured as phi.

query.search: ("integrated information" OR "integrated information theory") AND consciousness

directions.now: After a public dispute over whether IIT is testable, the work is on formal limits of phi, testable predictions such as 'silent neurons', and a new adversarial test against predictive processing.
directions.us: Our phi-proxy study checks whether the cheap stand-ins for phi used on real data track true phi.

directions.name: Higher-order and metacognitive theories
directions.bet: A state is conscious when the brain represents itself as being in it, so confidence and metacognition are the signal.

query.search: ("higher-order theory" OR "higher-order theories" OR "higher-order thought" OR "higher-order representation" OR "perceptual reality monitoring" OR ((metacognition OR metacognitive) AND (perception OR perceptual OR confidence OR visual))) AND consciousness

groups.name: David Soto
groups.inst: Basque Center on Cognition, Brain and Language

directions.now: The work centres on metacognition: whether confidence and prefrontal cortex are needed for awareness, building on relative-blindsight tasks.
directions.us: Our theory scorecard maps where this view and its rivals predict different results.

directions.name: Global workspace
directions.bet: Consciousness is information broadcast across the whole brain, with a sudden 'ignition' when something becomes conscious.

query.search: ("global workspace" OR "global neuronal workspace") AND consciousness

groups.name: Theofanis Panagiotaropoulos
groups.inst: National and Kapodistrian University of Athens

directions.now: The first adversarial test against IIT (Cogitate, 2025) failed some predictions of both theories; groups are reanalysing that data and asking whether language models build a workspace.
directions.us: Our sealed multiverse reanalysis of the Cogitate data tests the workspace and IIT predictions again.

directions.name: Adversarial collaborations
directions.bet: Rival theories agree on a decisive experiment before the data are in.

groups.name: Lucía Melloni
groups.inst: Max Planck Institute for Empirical Aesthetics

directions.now: Cogitate (workspace against IIT) has reported; INTREPID (IIT against predictive processing) is under way, and people are debating how to score theories fairly.
directions.us: We run sealed, pre-registered reanalyses of the open Cogitate data in the same spirit.

items.head: Waveform morphology links local circuit kinetics to cortical interactions
items.who: Núñez P, Kumar G, Gotti C, Wang P, Martineau L, Bonaventure PL, Hoyer R, Mišić B, Albouy P, Laureys S, Tewarie PKB
items.gist: The shape of a brain wave, not only its size, can make it look 'irreversible' in time.
items.plain: Brain waves are not perfect sine waves; their rise and fall can differ. This team showed in a model, in recordings from inside the brains of 23 patients and in monkeys, that this lopsidedness comes from how fast local synapses switch on and off. That lopsidedness was what most strongly drove a common measure of time-irreversibility.
items.tech: Modified Wilson-Cowan model; sEEG in 23 patients; macaque ECoG. Waveform asymmetry was most strongly associated with local irreversibility; alpha frequency related more to inter-regional measures. Phase-locked perturbations changed imaginary coherency and irreversibility with coupling fixed. Macaque ECoG reproduced the frequency links but not the waveform link. Not peer reviewed. (abstract only)
items.borrow: A likely reason for our own result: our waveform-asymmetry marker separated wake from deep sleep but not dreaming from deep sleep. If asymmetry reflects synaptic kinetics, it should follow arousal, which is what we saw.

items.head: Neural correlates of dreaming during N2 sleep: spatial and phenomenological characteristics
items.who: Rochas V, Mammeri K, Bayer L, Tononi G, Perogamvros L
items.gist: In light sleep, faster brain activity at the back of the head came before awakenings with a dream.
items.plain: Thirty-nine people slept with 256 electrodes on their heads and were woken many times from light (N2) sleep. When they said they had been dreaming, the seconds before waking showed more fast activity, strongest at the back of the brain. How much the dream felt like thinking mattered more than how much it felt like seeing.
items.tech: 39 participants, 256-channel EEG with source localisation, serial awakenings in N2. Experience with recall vs no experience: higher beta/gamma, widely distributed; peak in posterior occipito-temporal cortex for the 30 s window and parietal cortex for the 20 s window. Thought-related, not perceptual, ratings were associated with EEG activity. One lab, no held-out test; title and framing changed across preprint versions. Not peer reviewed. (abstract only)
items.borrow: Our experience benchmark uses the same stage (N2) and the last 20 s. A high-frequency effect like this one is what our frozen spectral baseline should already capture, so the question we ask is whether any other marker adds to it in labs it has never seen.

items.head: Individualised electrophysiological neural field models for the assessment of thalamocortical function in disorders of consciousness
items.who: Cóngyǔ L, Tewarie PKB, Alnagger NLN, Mindlin I, Van der Lande GJM, Belloli L, Laureys S, Naccache L, Rohaut B, Thibaut A, Annen J, Gosseries O, Núñez P, Sitt JD
items.gist: A brain model fitted only to EEG power reproduced the complexity scores that separate patients.
items.plain: Researchers fitted a model of the loop between the thalamus and the cortex to the EEG of more than 500 people with severe brain injury or none. The fitted loops were weaker in patients, weakest in the least responsive. The model was fitted only to how much power the EEG had at each frequency, yet the signals it produced had the same complexity scores as the real ones.
items.tech: Two independent high-density EEG datasets: 203 UWS, 270 MCS, 74 controls. Robinson corticothalamic neural field model fitted per person to spectra. Reduced corticothalamic integrity, UWS < MCS. Simulated EEG reproduced empirical complexity; permutation entropy separated MCS from UWS in real and simulated data. Code and replication data on GitHub.
items.borrow: Support for our main caution: if a model fitted to the spectrum reproduces a complexity score, that score adds little beyond the spectrum. We will check whether the shared replication data include per-patient spectra.

items.head: Inferring brain structural complexity from dynamical measures
items.who: Gaglioti G, Cattani A, Nieus T, Momi D, Comolatti R, Dalla Porta L, Sarasso S, Massimini M
items.gist: In simulated brains, pulse-based complexity tracked the wiring; measures of resting activity did not agree with each other.
items.plain: The team built simulated brains whose wiring they could change step by step, from orderly to random. Measures based on giving the network a kick peaked when wiring was in between, as theory expects. Measures taken from resting activity went different ways: some followed one property of the wiring, some another, some hardly moved.
items.tech: Wilson-Cowan mean-field networks with systematic rewiring. Observational metrics were heterogeneous (integration-tracking, differentiation-tracking, or insensitive). Perturbational metrics peaked at intermediate rewiring, scaled with small-worldness, resisted common-driver confounds and were highest near a wake-like regime. Simulation only; not peer reviewed. (abstract only)
items.borrow: A model-based reason the resting-EEG markers in our benchmark may fail. It also suggests a positive control we could add later: plant known wiring in a simulation and check each marker can see it.

items.head: Rapid alternation of conscious and suppressed stimulus representations in the primate brain
items.who: Hesse JK, Lanfranchi FF, McGrory C, Shi Y, Engel TA, Tsao DY
items.gist: Even while a monkey saw one steady image, face-selective neurons switched about 15 times a second between the seen image and the hidden one.
items.plain: Two images went to the two eyes, but only one was seen. Recording many neurons at once, the team found that the brain did not settle on the seen image. It flipped about 15 times a second between brief moments that carried the seen image and moments that carried the hidden one. In the 'seen' moments, neurons were more sharply tuned.
items.tech: Macaque Neuropixels recordings across IT face patches and prefrontal cortex during binocular flash suppression. Alternation at about 15 Hz between conscious and suppressed micro-epochs, each allowing image reconstruction; tuning amplified in conscious epochs; PFC qualitatively similar. Not peer reviewed. (abstract only)
items.borrow: A strong content result for our constraint ledger and theory scorecard. Not testable on the open human data we use.

items.head: Have grand theories of consciousness earned their keep?
items.who: Owen AM, Goodale MA
items.gist: Two senior researchers argue that careful experiments, not big theories, produced the field's real advances.
items.plain: This short opinion piece looks back at what moved consciousness science forward, such as finding hidden awareness in unresponsive patients. The authors argue those advances came from careful experiments rather than from the large theories that now get most attention.
items.tech: Perspective. Argues that future progress may depend on a return to the empirical tradition rather than adjudicating between overarching theories. (abstract only)
items.borrow: Matches how we work: a measure has to earn its place on held-out data before any theory is credited. Our main study is a benchmark, not a theory test, for this reason.

items.head: Neural signatures of conscious experience during sleep: a serial awakening study using high-density EEG
items.who: Selte A, Haworth SE, Vanasse TJ, Alauddin T, Gjini K, Philibert-Rosas S, Brace C, Sevak B, Riedner B, Kalkach-Aparicio M, Tononi G, Boly M, Struck AF
items.gist: A large sleep study reports that one minute of EEG can tell a dream from no dream about 80% of the time.
items.plain: A team woke 140 people about 700 times from non-REM sleep and asked whether anything had been going through their minds. Half the time the answer was yes. A computer, trained on the minute of brain signals before each awakening, picked the yes answers well above chance. Dreaming went with less slow activity and more fast activity at the back of the head. The study mixed light and deep sleep, and deep sleep is where 'nothing' answers are most common, so part of the signal may be sleep depth.
items.tech: 140 participants, 256-channel EEG, 699 N2 and N3 awakenings (351 experience, 348 no experience). Features from the 60 s before awakening: regional spectral power, lagged coherence, graph metrics, gamma/alpha ratios. Participant-level cross-validation. Best ensemble ROC-AUC 0.80, average precision 0.80. Dreaming: lower posterior alpha and delta, higher gamma-related measures. N2 and N3 pooled; one lab; no spectral-baseline nesting or surrogate control. Not peer reviewed. (abstract only; the full text was behind a bot block, which we did not get around)
items.borrow: This is the strongest claim yet that our main study could come out the other way. Our benchmark holds stage fixed, tests in labs never used for training, and asks what each marker adds over the spectrum. We will report the spectral baseline's own score as a headline number, so a strong spectral result is visible, not hidden.

items.head: Psychedelics align brain activity with context
items.who: Stoliker D, Novelli L, Khajehnejad M, Biabani M, Greaves MD, et al., Carhart-Harris RL, Seth AK, Sundram S, Egan GF, Razi A
items.gist: Psilocybin made brain activity follow what people were doing more closely, and the data are open.
items.plain: Sixty-two adults had brain scans and EEG while resting, meditating, listening to music and watching a film, once before and once on psilocybin. On the drug, brain activity moved along more structured paths that changed with the task. People who felt most 'embedded' in the world showed networks joining up that usually keep inner and outer processing apart.
items.tech: 62 adults; fMRI about 80 min and 64-channel EEG about 150 min after dose; rest, meditation, music and movie; low-dimensional trajectory analysis. Context-sensitive, structured trajectories co-varied with experience. Open data on OpenNeuro ds006110 (v1.2.0). Single site; EEG recorded later than fMRI.
items.borrow: Open EEG from a state where experience grows while arousal does not fall. That is the contrast our state benchmark lacks: a marker that rises here and falls under propofol is tracking more than wakefulness.

items.head: Systematic theory-method dependencies in consciousness research
items.who: Overgaard M, Dietz M, Waade PT
items.gist: Across 518 experiments, the method a study used predicted which theory it ended up supporting.
items.plain: If theories competed on the same ground, the kind of experiment run should not predict which theory wins. This team coded 518 experiments and found that it does: each theory lives in its own corner of methods, and is mostly tested there.
items.tech: Updated ConTraSt database, 518 experiments; Bayesian regression of support, challenge or no mention on methodological features. Decisive evidence for theory-method dependencies; partly separate methodological niches. Not peer reviewed. (abstract only)
items.borrow: Our theory scorecard will note which method each piece of evidence came from, so a theory is not credited just because its supporters favour one kind of experiment.

items.head: Thermodynamics of consciousness: non-equilibrium brain dynamics track conscious states
items.who: Berjaga-Buisan T, Monti JM, Cortada M, Colombo MA, Geli SM, Gaglioti G, Sarasso S, Kringelbach ML, Corbetta M, Sanchez-Vives MV, Massimini M, Perl YS, Deco G
items.gist: How far the brain sits from equilibrium tracked anaesthesia depth as well as the best-tested consciousness index.
items.plain: A brain at rest is never in balance: activity has a direction in time. This team fitted computer models to recordings from people and mice and measured how far each brain was from balance. The distance shrank under anaesthesia and in unresponsive patients. In mice it followed anaesthesia depth slightly more closely than the stimulation-based index does.
items.tech: Whole-brain generative models; fluctuation-dissipation theorem (FDT) violations from spontaneous activity. Mice under graded anaesthesia (LFP): PCI vs depth Spearman 0.71; FDT violations vs depth 0.885; FDT vs PCI 0.68. Lower FDT violations in unresponsive DoC and anaesthesia. Mouse data open on EBRAINS (10.25493/WKA8-Q4T). No spectral baseline.
items.borrow: We tested the scalp version of this idea (second-order irreversibility) on open sleep EEG and it did not replicate; our own time-asymmetry marker tracked arousal, not experience. The model-based estimator in this paper is still untested by us.

items.head: Verbalizable representations form a global workspace in language models
items.who: Gurnee W, Sofroniew N, Pearce A, Piotrowski M, Kauvar I, Chen R, Soligo A, Bogdan P, et al.
items.gist: Inside language models, the content a model can put into words behaves like a 'global workspace'.
items.plain: One leading theory says we are conscious of what is broadcast across the brain so many systems can use it. This study found a part of a language model's inner activity that holds what the model is about to say. That content can be reported, held, used for silent reasoning and shared widely, much as the theory describes for brains. This shows a working parallel, not that the model feels anything.
items.tech: A 'Jacobian lens' identifies a J-space of verbalisable representations. Its contents can be reported, summoned, held, used for silent reasoning and passed to downstream computation; coherent only in a middle band of layers; holds tens of concepts; more widely broadcast than other representations. Not peer reviewed. (abstract only)
items.borrow: A concrete, checkable workspace signature in AI. It fits the access side of the workspace theory and says nothing about experience; we would list it as an indicator, not evidence of consciousness.

items.head: Adversarial testing of global neuronal workspace and integrated information theories of consciousness
items.who: Cogitate Consortium (Ferrante, Gorska-Klimowska, Henin, Hirschhorn, Khalaf, Lepauvre, Liu, Richter, Vidal and others)
items.gist: The first big head-to-head test of two theories of consciousness found that each got some predictions right and each got key claims wrong.
items.plain: Two rival theories agreed in advance what results would count against them. Then 256 people looked at pictures while their brains were scanned in three different ways. Neither theory won. One theory said the back of the brain should stay in sync for as long as a picture is seen; it did not. The other said the front of the brain should flare up when a picture disappears; mostly it did not.
items.tech: n = 256 (fMRI 120, MEG 102, iEEG 34), suprathreshold faces, objects, letters and false fonts shown for 0.5, 1.0 or 1.5 s, task-relevant and task-irrelevant. Content information found in visual, ventrotemporal and inferior frontal cortex; sustained responses in occipital and lateral temporal cortex tracked duration; content-specific synchronisation between frontal and early visual areas. IIT challenged by no sustained posterior synchronisation; GNWT challenged by general lack of offset ignition and limited prefrontal representation of some conscious dimensions. Preregistration: osf.io/92tbg. Data CC BY 4.0, account needed for download.
items.borrow: The data is public (Experiment 1: MEG, fMRI, iEEG), so it is the first place we test whether the published conclusions survive other reasonable analyses. Note the paper's iEEG n is 34; the plan said 38.

items.head: Integrated information and predictive processing theories of consciousness: an adversarial collaborative review (INTREPID)
items.who: Corcoran AW, Haun AM, Dorman R, Tononi G, Friston KJ, Pennartz CMA, TWCF INTREPID Consortium
items.gist: The second big adversarial collaboration has published its plan: IIT against two predictive-brain theories. No results yet.
items.plain: Three teams with rival theories wrote down, together, which experiments would tell their ideas apart and what each result would mean. The experiments run across several labs. This paper is the agreed plan and a comparison of the theories, not the results.
items.tech: Compares IIT, neurorepresentationalism (Pennartz) and active inference (Friston): target phenomena, explanatory styles, methods. Lists key hypotheses for multi-site experiments and what would support or challenge each theory, and proposes formally combining results across experiments and replications into a quantitative measure of evidential support per theory. Preprint arXiv:2509.00555 (v1 Aug 2025, v3 May 2026). Online 14 May 2026, issue Aug 2026.
items.borrow: If its data appears after we seal our predictions, it is a clean prospective test. Its evidence-pooling idea is a model for our own log-score comparison of theories.

items.head: Testing the spatiotemporal predictions of global neuronal workspace theory and integrated information theory
items.who: Bandara KH, Rowe EG, Garrido MI
items.gist: A re-analysis of the COGITATE brain recordings finds the frontal 'flare-up' at picture offset that the original analysis missed.
items.plain: The same public data, analysed with a different method that asks which brain area drives which, gives a different answer from the original paper on one key point. This is a warning: with this much freedom in how to analyse the data, the conclusion can depend on the method.
items.tech: Dynamic causal modelling on the COGITATE MEG data (N = 100), task-irrelevant faces, split discovery-validation, expanding time windows. Support for GNWT's prefrontal ignition at both onset and offset (offset not seen in the original analyses). For IIT, fusiform-V1 feedback was not sustained, but intrinsic fusiform connectivity was broadly consistent with sustained processing; a post-hoc face-vs-object validation gave no strong evidence of face selectivity (pp < 0.95), so the IIT findings are read conservatively. Not peer reviewed.
items.borrow: This is the 'July 2026 reanalysis' the plan could not name. It goes into our multiverse on COGITATE (task #11) as one of the analysis paths, and shows why we hash the analysis set first.

items.head: A data-driven approach to identifying and evaluating connectivity-based neural correlates of conscious visual perception
items.who: Bryant AG, Whyte CJ
items.gist: Testing 246 ways of measuring brain connectivity on the COGITATE data gives tentative support to the workspace theory.
items.plain: Rather than pick one connectivity measure, the authors tried 246 of them on the same public recordings, found the family that best tells pictures apart, and then built small brain models of each theory to see which reproduced it. Both models fit; the authors lean slightly towards the workspace theory.
items.tech: COGITATE MEG, 94 of 100 downloaded participants with anatomy for source localisation. 246 functional connectivity measures between IIT- and GNWT-predicted regions; barycenter-based measures decoded stimuli best and generalised across regions. Neural mass models: GNWT with delayed ignition, IIT with synchronous sensory dynamics; both captured the observed patterns. Conclusion: tentative support for GNWT, because ignition appeared regardless of task demands. A correction was issued (niag071).
items.borrow: A second independent reanalysis of the same data, from a different angle. Its 246-measure sweep is a template for our pre-registered multiverse; we would hash the measure list first.

items.head: A dream EEG and mentation database (DREAM)
items.who: Wong W, Herzog R, Andrade KC, Andrillon T and others; senior author Tsuchiya N
items.gist: Twenty sleep studies pooled their brain recordings with what people said they were dreaming when woken up: 505 people, 2,643 awakenings.
items.plain: When you wake someone in the night and ask what was going through their mind, sometimes they report a dream and sometimes nothing. Single labs could only collect a few hundred of these. This database pools them, so we can ask, with far more data, whether brain signals before waking predict a dream report.
items.tech: Initial release: 20 datasets, 505 participants, 2,643 awakenings; each has sleep M/EEG (>= 20 s, >= 100 Hz, >= 2 electrodes) up to waking plus a standardised report class. Experience vs no experience decoded from EEG over 200 random train-test splits against a label-shuffled null: NREM best with spectral power features (mean AUC 0.586, 5th-95th percentile 0.505-0.608); REM best with catch22 features (mean AUC 0.700, 0.663-0.731). Six datasets used for these analyses. Registry open (doi:10.26180/22133105); dataset packages either open access or by request from the contributor. Main text does not say whether splits held out whole subjects.
items.borrow: The key resource for our dream vs no-dream test (task #6). Their AUCs are the bar to beat, but we split by subject and lab, so our numbers may come out lower.

items.head: A repeated awakening study exploring the capacity of complexity measures to capture dreaming during propofol sedation
items.who: Bajwa IJ, Nilsen AS, Skukies R, Aamodt A, Ernst G, Storm JF, Juel BE
items.gist: Brain complexity dropped under sedation, but did not differ between people who said they had been dreaming and people who said they had not.
items.plain: Twenty volunteers were sedated and woken several times to ask whether they had experienced anything. Complexity measures fell with sedation as expected. But they did not tell 'I was dreaming' from 'nothing' within sedation. Only 5 wakings gave a clear 'nothing', so the test could only have caught a large difference.
items.tech: 20 healthy participants, propofol, resting EEG and TMS-EEG (PCIst) plus single-channel LZc. 52 attempted awakenings: 24 experience, 5 no experience, 23 unarousable or uninformative. Both measures fell from wake to sedation; no evidence of a difference between experience and no-experience awakenings within sedation (linear mixed models). Data: OpenNeuro ds005620 v1.0.0, CC0, 21 subjects, 83.0 GB in full (OpenNeuro metadata).
items.borrow: One of our L2 datasets. The full set is far over our 1.5 GB budget; we fetch only the pre-awakening sedation files per subject. The 5 no-experience awakenings make it weak alone for dream vs no-dream; pool with DREAM.

items.head: The role of etiology in the identification of clinical markers of consciousness: comparing EEG alpha power, complexity, and spectral exponent
items.who: Maschke C, Belloli L, Manasova D, Sitt JD, Blain-Moraes S
items.gist: In 303 unresponsive patients, a popular complexity measure mostly repeated what the slope of the EEG spectrum already showed; once corrected for that, its diagnostic value vanished.
items.plain: A brain 'complexity' score is often used as a sign of consciousness. Here it moved almost in lockstep with a much simpler property of the signal, how fast power falls off with frequency. When the authors compared each recording with scrambled copies that keep that property, the complexity score stopped telling patients apart. Which marker worked also depended on the cause of brain injury.
items.tech: 303 unresponsive patients. Shuffle-normalised LZC correlated with the 1-40 Hz spectral exponent at r(197) = 0.86; phase-normalising (surrogates with matched spectrum) reduced this to r(197) = 0.24, and all LZC diagnostic effects vanished; partialling out the exponent did the same. Alpha power had more diagnostic value in anoxic patients; spectral slope only in non-anoxic patients. Code: github.com/BIAPT/Markers.
items.borrow: The direct source for our surrogate gate (task #8) and the LZ vs slope test (task #4). It is the PMC12448740 paper the plan cites. We also stratify by aetiology wherever patient data allow.

items.head: Critical dynamics in spontaneous EEG predict perturbational complexity in disorders of consciousness with measurable evoked responses
items.who: Newman D, Maschke C, O'Byrne J, Colombo MA, Comanducci A, Casarotto S, Citerio G, Rosanova M, Massimini M, Jerbi K, Blain-Moraes S
items.gist: Resting brain signals could stand in for the stimulation-based consciousness index in some brain-injured patients, but not across all of them.
items.plain: The best-tested consciousness index needs a magnetic pulse to the head. This team asked whether ordinary resting EEG can predict it in 26 brain-injured patients. It could not across the whole group, only in patients whose injury was not from lack of oxygen and in those with a measurable response.
items.tech: 26 patients (vascular, traumatic, anoxic). Multivariate criticality features did not generalise PCImax prediction across the full cohort; they did when restricted to non-anoxic patients and to patients with non-zero PCImax. Extends Maschke et al. 2024 (anaesthesia) to brain injury. Not peer reviewed.
items.borrow: Tempers the 2024 claim that resting EEG can replace PCI. Our out-of-sample test of that claim should report results by aetiology.

items.head: Convergent transcriptomic and connectomic controllers of information integration and its anaesthetic breakdown across mammalian brains
items.who: Luppi AI, Uhrig L, Tasserie J, Mediano PAM, Rosas FE and others; senior author Stamatakis EA
items.gist: Across humans, monkeys, marmosets and mice, anaesthetics break down the brain's integration of information, and waking a monkey with deep-brain stimulation brings it back.
items.plain: Brain scans under anaesthesia in four species show the same thing: information stops being combined across the brain. In monkeys, stimulating the thalamus reawakened them and restored it. This points the opposite way from a 2024 rat EEG study where an integration estimate went up under anaesthesia.
items.tech: fMRI with anaesthesia in humans, macaques, marmosets and mice. Breakdown of integrated information is a convergent effect of diverse anaesthetics; dynamics become harder to control; both reversed by thalamic DBS-induced awakening in macaque. Regional breakdown follows PVALB expression topography; species-specific computational models.
items.borrow: Shows that whether a Phi-like proxy rises or falls under anaesthesia depends on the modality and the estimator. Our known-Phi network test (task #9) must check each proxy before we trust its direction.

items.head: Identifying indicators of consciousness in AI systems
items.who: Butlin P, Long R, Bayne T, Bengio Y, Birch J, Chalmers D and others (20 authors)
items.gist: A method for judging whether an AI could be conscious by checking its inner workings against what theories of consciousness require, not by what it says.
items.plain: Instead of asking a chatbot whether it feels anything, the authors take the core requirements of several brain theories and check whether an AI system's internal machinery meets them. This builds on their 2023 report, which concluded that no current AI system was a strong candidate.
items.tech: Four guidelines for deriving indicators, e.g. indicators should target the central explanatory posits of a theory; illustrated with the indicator list from the 2023 report (arXiv:2308.08708, 19 authors, which drew on recurrent processing, global workspace, higher-order, predictive processing and attention schema theories and concluded no current AI systems are conscious but saw no obvious technical barriers to meeting the indicators). Issue June 2026 (vol 30, issue 6).
items.borrow: The rubric for our AI stress tests: we use it to find where theories disagree or give absurd answers, never as a verdict on AI and never scoring an AI's self-report.

items.head: Electrophysiological effects of psilocybin co-administered with midazolam
items.who: Sutherland M, Nicholas C, Lennertz R, Wenthur C and others
items.gist: With a sedative given alongside psilocybin, brain-signal complexity still rose as the psychedelic effects came on.
items.plain: Psilocybin was given together with a sedative that blunts memory. Early on, when mainly the sedative was acting, the EEG looked sedated. As the psychedelic took hold over six hours, complexity rose and power fell, and these changes tracked people's ratings of altered experience better than ratings of sedation.
items.tech: Oral psilocybin 25 mg plus IV midazolam, high-density EEG. At 15-30 min (midazolam at target, psilocybin likely not): higher beta power, lower spectral exponent. Over the next six hours: higher normalised LZC and spectral exponent, lower broadband power. OAA/S sedation scores improved model fits for alpha power; ASC items improved fits for LZCn and spectral exponent. Small open-label pilot. Preprint bioRxiv 10.1101/2025.07.25.666887.
items.borrow: A case where complexity and the spectral exponent move together under a drug that changes experience. Our test asks whether complexity adds anything once the exponent is known.

items.head: Critical dynamics in spontaneous EEG predict anesthetic-induced loss of consciousness and perturbational complexity
items.who: Maschke C, O'Byrne J, Colombo MA, Boly M, Gosseries O, Laureys S, Rosanova M, Jerbi K, Blain-Moraes S
items.gist: In 15 healthy adults under three anaesthetics, resting EEG predicted the stimulation-based consciousness index closely.
items.plain: Volunteers were put under with propofol, xenon or ketamine; all stopped responding, but only the ketamine group reported vivid dreams afterwards. Measures of how close the resting brain sits to a 'critical' tipping point separated the dreaming group from the others, and predicted each person's score on the magnetic-pulse test.
items.tech: 15 healthy adults (propofol 5, xenon 5, ketamine 5), data from earlier studies. Avalanche criticality, chaoticity and related metrics; unconsciousness moved away from criticality and the edge of chaos. Ridge regression on 16 features predicted PCImax; leave-one-subject-out (15 folds) mean absolute error 0.065 (+/- 0.042); a 0.35 threshold separated conscious and unconscious states for true and predicted PCImax.
items.borrow: If true, the best-validated measure could be tested on many more open datasets. Caution: 15 subjects, 5 per drug, and the same cohort as Colombo 2019 and Sarasso 2015, so these are not independent replications. We test it out of sample.

items.head: Exploring effects of anesthesia on complexity, differentiation, and integrated information in rat EEG
items.who: Nilsen AS, Arena A, Storm JF
items.gist: In rats, integrated-information estimates from spontaneous EEG went up under anaesthesia, opposite to the stimulation-based index.
items.plain: The researchers compared a stimulation-based complexity score with several scores computed from ordinary EEG in rats under three anaesthetics. Some scores worked well. But the estimates of 'integrated information', the quantity at the heart of one major theory, generally rose under propofol and sevoflurane, the reverse of what that theory expects.
items.tech: Rats under propofol, sevoflurane and ketamine. PCI (electrical stimulation), LZ and geometric integrated information (PhiG) best separated wake from propofol and sevoflurane. PCI was anti-correlated with spontaneous integrated-information measures, which generally increased under propofol and sevoflurane. Authors suggest perturbation-based and spontaneous measures may be complementary.
items.borrow: A warning that Phi proxies may not track what IIT says Phi tracks. Our known-Phi network test checks this before any proxy touches brain data.

items.head: The integrated information theory of consciousness as pseudoscience
items.who: IIT-Concerned, Fleming SM, Frith CD and others
items.venue: PsyArXiv (open letter); follow-up in Nature Neuroscience 28, 689-693 (2025)
items.gist: A group of researchers called IIT pseudoscience, which set off a public dispute over what counts as a test of a theory of consciousness.
items.plain: After press coverage called IIT a leading, tested theory, researchers wrote an open letter objecting. In 2025 a follow-up in Nature Neuroscience argued the theory's core claims cannot be tested even in principle. The row is about what a fair test of a theory of consciousness looks like.
items.tech: Letter posted 16 Sep 2023 on PsyArXiv. Follow-up: IIT-Concerned et al., 'What makes a theory of consciousness unscientific?', Nature Neuroscience 28, 689-693, doi:10.1038/s41593-025-01881-x (104 author entries in Crossref, including the collective name). We did not verify the number of signatories on the 2023 letter.
items.borrow: It is why we judge every theory only by predictions sealed in advance.

items.head: Integrated information theory (IIT) 4.0: formulating the properties of phenomenal existence in physical terms
items.who: Albantakis L, Barbosa L, Findlay G, Grasso M, Haun AM and others; senior author Tononi G
items.gist: The current formal version of integrated information theory.
items.plain: IIT starts from what experience is like and works out what a physical system must be like to have it, then puts that in mathematics. In principle the maths says whether any system is conscious and how. In practice it cannot be computed for a brain, so only rough stand-ins can be tested.
items.tech: Axioms to postulates to mathematical expressions; a unique measure of intrinsic information consistent with the postulates; explicit treatment of causal relations; a system's unfolded cause-effect structure accounts for the quality of experience.
items.borrow: The reference for the IIT row on our scoreboard and for which toy networks have exactly computable Phi in our planted-answer tests.

items.head: The neural correlates of dreaming
items.who: Siclari F, Baird B, Perogamvros L, Bernardi G, LaRocque JJ, Riedner B, Boly M, Postle BR, Tononi G
items.gist: Less slow activity at the back of the brain marked dreaming in both kinds of sleep, and could predict a dream report in real time.
items.plain: People were woken many times a night and asked if they had been dreaming. In both dreaming-heavy and dreaming-light stages of sleep, a dream report followed a drop in slow brain waves over a 'hot zone' at the back of the head. Watching that zone live predicted whether the sleeper would report a dream.
items.tech: High-density EEG, serial awakenings. Dream reports in NREM and REM associated with local decreases in low-frequency activity in posterior cortex; high-frequency activity there correlated with specific dream contents; real-time monitoring predicted dream vs no-dream reports in NREM.
items.borrow: The sharpest within-stage test of a measure against report. The DREAM database (2025) lets us test whether it replicates across labs.

items.head: Stratification of unresponsive patients by an independently validated index of brain complexity
items.who: Casarotto S, Comanducci A, Rosanova M and others; senior author Massimini M
items.gist: A cutoff on the stimulation-based complexity index, set in people who could report, separated conscious from unconscious perfectly and flagged some 'vegetative' patients as possibly conscious.
items.plain: The team first set a threshold using 150 people whose state was known from their own reports. That threshold then caught almost all minimally conscious patients, and showed 9 of 43 patients judged vegetative with scores like conscious people.
items.tech: Benchmark population 150 (healthy and communicative brain-injured; wake, disconnected consciousness, unconsciousness). Optimal cutoff gave 100% sensitivity and specificity in the benchmark; applied to 38 MCS and 43 VS patients: 94.7% sensitivity for MCS; 9 of 43 VS patients above the cutoff.
items.borrow: The strongest published L2 result. No open TMS-EEG set of this kind exists, which is the biggest data gap in our plan.

items.head: A theoretically based index of consciousness independent of sensory processing and behavior (PCI)
items.who: Casali AG, Gosseries O, Rosanova M, Boly M, Sarasso S and others; senior author Massimini M
items.gist: The paper that introduced the perturbational complexity index: tap the brain with a magnetic pulse and measure how complex the echo is.
items.plain: If a brain is both well connected and varied, a magnetic pulse should set off a rich, hard-to-compress pattern of activity. The score built on that idea separated wake from deep sleep and anaesthesia in single people, and tracked recovery in patients emerging from coma.
items.tech: TMS-evoked EEG responses compressed (Lempel-Ziv) after source modelling and binarisation. Tested in wake, dreaming, NREM sleep, midazolam, xenon and propofol sedation, and in vegetative, minimally conscious and locked-in patients; discriminated level of consciousness in single individuals.
items.borrow: The measure every spontaneous-EEG candidate is judged against.

items.head: Consciousness and complexity during unresponsiveness induced by propofol, xenon, and ketamine
items.who: Sarasso S, Boly M, Napolitani M and others; senior author Massimini M
items.gist: Under ketamine, people stopped responding but their brain's response to a magnetic pulse stayed wake-like, and afterwards they reported vivid dreams.
items.plain: Three anaesthetics all made volunteers unresponsive. After propofol and xenon they remembered nothing. After ketamine they described long, vivid dreams, and during it the brain's response to stimulation stayed complex like in waking. This is the classic case where behaviour and experience come apart.
items.tech: 18 healthy volunteers. Frontal and parietal TMS: propofol gave a local low-complexity slow wave, xenon a global stereotyped low-complexity slow wave, ketamine a wake-like complex pattern. Reports on emergence: none after propofol and xenon; long vivid dreams after ketamine.
items.borrow: Defines our ketamine dissociation case. The same group's data underlies Colombo 2019 and Maschke 2024, so we need an independent ketamine dataset.

items.head: Increased spontaneous MEG signal diversity for psychoactive doses of ketamine, LSD and psilocybin
items.who: Schartner MM, Carhart-Harris RL, Barrett AB, Seth AK, Muthukumaraswamy SD
items.gist: Psychedelics pushed brain-signal diversity above normal waking levels, the first time such measures went higher than wakefulness.
items.plain: Complexity scores are usually highest in normal waking. Under psilocybin, ketamine and LSD they went higher still, and some of the rise tracked how intense people said the experience was.
items.tech: Spontaneous MEG; LZ and entropy measures higher for all three drugs, even when controlling for spectral changes; strongest for single-channel LZ (temporal diversity). Selective correlations with phenomenological intensity ratings.
items.borrow: Tests whether a measure rises when contents intensify but level does not obviously change. We re-check the spectral control with phase-randomised surrogates.
